results.title: H100 Rental Prices Halve to $3.43/Hr in 2026
highlights:
Renting an Nvidia H100 for an hour costs anywhere from $1.30 an hour to as much as $12.29 in October 2026 according to Coloprice, depending on who you ask and which cloud you pick, with GPUFinder naming Lium as the cheapest confirmed H100 at $1.79 an hour and GPU marketplace tracker Uvik putting the median H100 SXM on-demand price at $4.20 across 16 surveyed providers on October 7. That spread, once a rounding error in a niche market, has become one of the clearest signals of how tight the AI compute supply chain still is, two years after ChatGPT turned GPU capacity into a boardroom talking point. Pricing trackers, bank analysts, and Nvidia’s own executives are now telling three overlapping stories at once: H100 rental costs have fallen by roughly half since early 2024, newer chips like the H200 and B200 command a steep premium, and the entire market remains bottlenecked by memory, not by silicon.

...

Pricing tracker Thunder Compute, in a blog post on H100 pricing dated September 1, 2026, lists on-demand H100 80GB rates spanning from $2.89 an hour on RunPod up to $10.98 an hour on Google Cloud’s a3-highgpu-8g instances. CloudZero’s own H100 cost breakdown, published in late August 2026, puts the low end at Vast.ai for as little as $1.49 an hour, though GPUFinder’s October 2026 listing of $1.29 an hour on Hyperbolic now sets the floor, while Rank.ai listed Azure H100 capacity at $6.98 to $12.29 per GPU-hour in October 2026, which stretches the spread at the top even wider. Between those two data points sits a real number that infrastructure teams have to budget against every quarter.

## Cloud GPU Rental Prices in September 2026: The Numbers

Three tiers have emerged in the market and they behave almost like separate products. Marketplace and community-cloud rates sit at the floor, where platforms like RunPod’s community tier and Vast.ai’s peer-to-peer listings undercut everyone else. Specialist clouds such as Lambda, Nebius, and Crusoe occupy the middle, offering more reliability and support without hyperscaler markup (Hyperstack was reported at $2.50 an hour for H100 on a rate checked October 31, 2026, and Modal at $3.9492 an hour on a rate checked October 26, 2026), though that tier is not static: Nebius reportedly increased its H100 price from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour effective October 1, 2026, a rise of about 16.9% that formed part of a rate-card increase of as much as 21%. Hyperscaler on-demand pricing from AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud sits at the top, often two to four times the marketplace floor for the exact same chip.

| Chip | Marketplace / community floor | Specialist cloud (mid-tier) | Hyperscaler on-demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 80GB | $1.49–$2.99/hr | $3.19–$4.59/hr | $6.88–$10.98/hr |
| H200 141GB | $3.59/hr (RunPod Community) | $4.31–$4.59/hr | $5.58–$6.35/hr |
| B200 | Limited public data | $5.89/hr (RunPod tier cited by Hackceleration) | $8.64/hr (normalized Flex estimate) |

Sourcing for that table pulls from Thunder Compute’s H200 pricing tracker, RunPod’s own published rate cards, and CloudZero’s cross-cloud comparison. B200 numbers remain the least reliable of the three chips. Nvidia has shipped Blackwell in volume since early 2026, but most cloud providers still quote B200 capacity through sales conversations rather than public rate cards, which is why independent trackers keep flagging the chip as data-scarce even six months after general availability.

...

## Nvidia H200: The 141GB Premium Tier

The H200 carries 141GB of HBM3e memory versus the H100’s 80GB, and cloud providers price that memory bump directly into the rental rate. RunPod’s community-cloud listing for H200 141GB has held at roughly $3.59 an hour through most of 2026, according to multiple pricing aggregators including DeployBase and Flexprice, while RunPod’s secure-cloud tier for the same chip runs $4.39 to $4.59 an hour. Hivenet’s own pricing page, updated August 28, 2026, lists H200 SXM configurations as high as $4.31 an hour for cluster-grade deployments, and Nebius lists H200 at $5.40 per GPU-hour effective October 1, 2026.

What stands out is how narrow the gap has become between H100 and H200 pricing at the top end. A specialist-cloud H100 at $4.59 an hour and an H200 at the same price point mean buyers increasingly default to the newer chip whenever the rate cards converge, since the extra memory headroom costs nothing extra at that tier. That dynamic is quietly pushing H100 demand down toward the marketplace floor, which is part of why sub-$2 H100 listings have become common on peer-to-peer platforms this year. RunPod itself listed H100 PCIe at $1.99 an hour on Community Cloud and $2.39 an hour on Secure Cloud in August 2026, and Rank.ai put Akash’s median H100 rental price at $2.56 an hour in October 2026.

## Nvidia B200 and Blackwell Ultra: Why Public Data Stays Thin

Blackwell-generation B200 chips reached general availability across major clouds in the first half of 2026, but transparent, per-hour rental pricing has been slow to show up on public rate cards. The clearest figures come from Bank of America’s tracking: Vivek Arya’s note put B200 spot pricing around $5.66 an hour as of mid-August 2026, while the TechFlowPost-covered BofA report from a week later listed B200 at $5.63 an hour, down 2% month over month but still up 7% from a year earlier.

Retail-style pricing trackers show a wider range. Lambda lists B200 at $6.69 per GPU-hour for an eight-GPU configuration, RunPod Secure Cloud at $7.99 and Hyperstack at $6.00, while Nebius reportedly charges $8.50 from October 1, 2026 (up from $7.15, an increase of approximately 18.9%), a provider-specific increase rather than a rate every B200 provider charges, CoreWeave’s eight-GPU HGX B200 instance works out to about $8.60 per GPU, and AWS sits at the top of the range at $14.24. A Nebius preemptible B200 listing was reported at $5.00 per GPU-hour in one region on October 29, 2026, though that figure is not directly comparable with on-demand pricing. Blackwell Ultra is priced publicly too: Nebius lists B300 at $9.50 from October 1, 2026, Verda at $8.20, Scaleway at $7.50 and Together AI at $9.99.

...

AIMultiple’s Cloud GPU Rental Price Index, updated August 25, 2026, found that the median H100 rental price across its tracked cohort now sits around $3.38 an hour, down from more than $7 an hour in early 2024. That is a genuine price collapse of over half in just two and a half years, and it reflects the normal pattern for an aging chip: more supply comes online, more providers compete for the same customers, and rates fall. A separate tracker tells a similar story from a slightly later vantage point: the Mercatus GPU Index, measured September 13, 2026, put the average H100 rate at $3.84 an hour across 27 tracked providers, with Lambda listing $3.99 an hour, a reminder that the exact figure depends heavily on which cohort and which averaging method a tracker uses. The GPU Rental Price Index at gpurentalprices.com, which read prices from 1 November 2026 to 6 November 2026, has H100 averaging $3.43 an hour for the month to date, a figure that sits between the AIMultiple and Mercatus readings.

...

results.title: Neoclouds vs Hyperscalers: GPU Cloud Models Compared
highlights:
Neoclouds — CoreWeave, Nebius, Lambda, Crusoe — are GPU-only cloud providers that rent Nvidia compute 40-85% below AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud list prices, but they finance that growth with debt and multi-year take-or-pay contracts rather than the diversified revenue and cash reserves that hyperscalers use. Both models sell GPU cycles; they differ in what else is on the menu, who is on the other side of the balance sheet, and how much counterparty risk a buyer takes on. Below is the data on pricing, financing, and where each model fits.

...

- Neocloud on-demand H100 pricing runs about $4.17/hr median versus roughly $7.89/hr averaged across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud — an 89% premium for hyperscaler-branded, identical Nvidia silicon, per Thunder Compute and GPUSmith trackers.
- The four largest hyperscalers plus Oracle are guiding to $660-690 billion in combined 2026 capital expenditure, roughly 77% above 2025’s ~$410 billion, per Futurum Group.
- CoreWeave’s total debt reached $35.6 billion by June 30, 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $5.13 billion — a debt-to-revenue ratio no hyperscaler carries against its cloud segment.
- Nebius signed $46 billion in combined capacity deals with Microsoft and Meta in 2026 and grew revenue 454% year over year to $582.3 million in Q2, with ARR reaching $3 billion.
- Synergy Research forecasts the neocloud market growing from roughly $25 billion in 2025 revenue to nearly $400 billion by 2031 — a 58% compound annual growth rate — even as hyperscalers grow their share of total data center capacity to 67% over the same period.
- The GPU depreciation debate (5-6 year hyperscaler schedules versus a 2-3 year real-world chip cycle) matters more for neoclouds, whose debt is often collateralized directly against the depreciating hardware.

...

| Provider | Type | Scale signal | Headline pricing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWS / Azure / Google Cloud | Hyperscaler | $660-690B combined 2026 capex (top 5 incl. Oracle) | H100 on-demand $6.88-12.29/hr |
| CoreWeave | Neocloud | FY2025 revenue $5.13B (+168%); Q1 2026 revenue $2.08B (+112%) | H100 PCIe ~$4.25/hr; reserved ~$1.45/hr |
| Nebius | Neocloud | Q2 2026 revenue $582.3M (+454%); ARR $3B | Contract-priced; avg. deal yield >$20M/MW |
| Lambda | Neocloud | H100 SXM $3.99-4.29/hr with 99.9% uptime SLA | H100 from $2.49/hr (no egress fees) |
| Crusoe | Neocloud | ~5 GW contracted AI infrastructure capacity (June 2026); $30B valuation | Build-to-suit and cloud, contract-priced |

## Pricing: the gap that defines the category

| GPU / metric | AWS | Azure | Google Cloud | Neocloud (typical) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 on-demand | $6.88/hr | $12.29/hr | $10.98/hr | ~$2.49-4.25/hr (Lambda, CoreWeave) |
| H100, reserved/committed | Lower with 1-3yr terms | Lower with 1-3yr terms | Lower with 1-3yr terms | ~$1.45/hr (CoreWeave reserved) |
| Egress fees | Standard hyperscaler rates | Standard hyperscaler rates | Standard hyperscaler rates | Often $0 (Lambda, RunPod) |
| Service catalog | Hundreds of services | Hundreds of services | Hundreds of services | GPU compute, storage, networking only |

...

Roughly 40-85% cheaper for identical silicon. On-demand H100 rates run about $6.88/hr on AWS, $10.98/hr on Google Cloud, and $12.29/hr on Azure, versus a neocloud median near $4.17/hr — Lambda at $2.49/hr, Spheron at $2.50/hr, and CoreWeave reserved capacity as low as $1.45/hr, per GPUSmith and Thunder Compute pricing trackers.

results.title: CFTC Opens the Door to Compute Futures With Formal Comment Request | AI2Work
highlights:
- 1 The CFTC's August 19 request for comment poses 23 numbered questions across four areas — cash market structure, manipulation risk, customer protection, and perpetual futures — but proposes no rules and approves no product. Comments close October 20, 2026.
- 2 The Commission's central worry is stated plainly in the document: compute may not yet exhibit the fungibility, standardization, and liquidity that commodities underlying derivatives markets normally have, and most economic value moves through private bilateral contracts that no index can observe.
- 3 Exchanges are not waiting. CME Group and Silicon Data have set October 5 for two cash-settled GPU rental index contracts, with ICE, Architect Financial Technologies, and Nodal Exchange all circling the same benchmark position.

On August 19, 2026, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission did something that looks procedural and

...

The timing matters more than the text. CME Group and Silicon Data have already announced two compute futures contracts targeting an October 5 launch, pending regulatory review. Intercontinental Exchange has its own partnerships. The Commission is asking foundational questions about whether compute can support a derivatives market at the same moment that exchanges are preparing to find out empirically.

...

The public price data supports the concern rather than dispelling it. Silicon Data's neo-cloud index has recently shown H100 capacity around $2.53 per GPU-hour. Bank of America research cited in August coverage put H100 spot rental closer to $2.77, up roughly a third year over year. SemiAnalysis has tracked one-year committed contracts moving the other way from spot, rising from about $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to roughly $2.35 by March 2026. Market surveys of published rates still show a spread running from under $1.50 on peer-to-peer marketplaces to double digits on the priciest hyperscaler listing for identical silicon.

...

| Venue | Index or partner | Product structure | Status as announced |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CME Group (listed under NYMEX rules) | Silicon Data H100 and B200 Rental Indexes | Cash-settled futures, each contract representing one month of rent for a single GPU | Targeting October 5, 2026, pending regulatory review |
| Intercontinental Exchange | Ornn Compute Price Index (OCPI) | USD-denominated, cash-settled GPU compute futures across major hardware types | Announced May 2026, subject to regulatory approval |
| Intercontinental Exchange | NATIVX | GPU compute futures positioned alongside existing power and natural gas contracts | Reported plans, 2026 |
| Architect Financial Technologies | In-house (AX platform) | Exchange-traded perpetual futures referencing GPU and RAM prices | Announced U.S. futures exchange for compute following a DCM acquisition, May 2026 |
| Nodal Exchange | Not disclosed | Futures on computing power for AI chips | Reported as seeking to launch |
| Kalshi | Not applicable | Event contracts on the direction of GPU compute prices | Reported as live; prediction-market structure, not a futures contract |

...

A request for comment is a consultation. It is not a rule, not a rulemaking proposal in substance, and not an approval of any product. Nothing in the text authorises any venue to list any compute contract, and October 20 is a deadline for submitting opinions rather than a date on which anything begins trading. Chairman Selig voted in the affirmative and no Commissioner voted against, which tells you the Commission is aligned on asking the questions — not that it has answered them. Treat any vendor claim that the CFTC has "greenlit" compute futures as marketing.

results.title: Is the 'Computing Power' That Powers AI Becoming a Financial Product? — Why a GPU Futures Market Is Beginning｜市場の地図
highlights:
CME Group, one of the world's largest derivatives exchanges, plans to launch futures linked to GPU rental prices on October 5, 2026. The underlying assets are NVIDIA's H100 and B200 AI-focused GPUs. The launch is subject to regulatory review and is not yet finalized.

...

According to data from Silicon Data, introduced by Reuters Breakingviews, the cost to use an NVIDIA H100 for one hour was $7.23 at major cloud providers and $2.65 at smaller cloud providers. There is a significant price difference depending on the source, even for the same type of GPU.

...

The GPU futures planned by CME are not contracts to receive the physical GPU in the future. They are a mechanism to trade on whether the future price of computing power will rise or fall, linked to the GPU hourly rental price index calculated by Silicon Data.

...

The futures that CME plans to handle first will be linked to the rental prices of NVIDIA's H100 and B200 chips.

This could mean more to NVIDIA than just selling GPUs. If market participants begin to compare the price of computing power based on the H100 and B200, NVIDIA GPUs are likely to become the de facto standard for AI computing power.

results.title: H100 Rentals Crashed 70%. Should You Still Buy the GPU? | bex.co
highlights:
Two years ago, renting a single Nvidia H100 cost roughly $8 to $10 per GPU-hour. Today you can get one for about $2.50. That is a 70% price collapse on the most important chip in AI infrastructure, and it quietly rewrote one of the standard arguments in platform engineering: at $8 an hour, buying your own GPU was obviously smart. At $2.50, the answer is genuinely unclear — and the breakeven point moved from “run it a quarter of the time” to “run it nearly around the clock.”

...

| Period | Typical H100 rental (per GPU-hour) | What was happening |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Late 2023 | $7–10, spiking above $12 on major clouds | Acute shortage; hyperscaler-only supply |
| Q4 2024 | $8–10 | Peak scarcity pricing |
| Q1 2025 | $5.50–7.00 | Supply improves as datacenter buildouts land |
| Q2 2025 | $3.50–4.50 | Neocloud capacity floods in |
| Late 2025 | $2.85–3.50 | Market stabilizes at a third of peak |
| 2026 | ~$2–3 on specialized clouds | Median on-demand about $2.99 |

...

Budget marketplaces list H100s from around $1.49 (Vast.ai) to $1.99 (RunPod); managed specialists like Lambda sit near $2.49–3.99; CoreWeave is around $4.25; hyperscalers still charge up to $6.88–6.98 per GPU-hour.

...

First, the crash is concentrated in on-demand rental on specialized clouds and marketplaces. Hyperscaler on-demand barely budged in comparison: AWS and Azure still charge roughly $7 per H100-hour, nearly triple the neocloud rate. If your workloads live inside a hyperscaler VPC with no exit plan, you have not experienced a 70% price cut. The glut pooled where new capacity was actually built — the neoclouds — and hyperscaler pricing lagged it by the usual 6–12 months, if it follows at all.
